chapter_theme: Under the heading பகைத்திறம் தெரிதல் (first part), thirteen verses on dealing with enemies: fear empties every fort, a young enmity must be cut off from its allies, retaliation must not wait, favours do not win a settled foe, the great and their dependents must not be provoked, the weak should flee and live, an old enemy never becomes a friend, and a false friend close by is worse than a flood afar.

285.reading: The verse asks whether anyone, by pouring in strength, can make those who lack a footing of their own stand in glory, even when they have strong backers, and answers that for those who fear there is no fortress, whoever they are.
285.nuance: The verse sets two supports against each other: வன்சார்பு, the strong backing of allies, and தஞ்சார்பு, a footing of one's own; the first cannot make up for the lack of the second. This reading takes both phrases of the same people; if தஞ்சார்பு இலாதாரை is instead the attacker's victims (those without allies of their own), the verse asks whether the strong may lord it over the friendless, and the proverb fits less well.
285.domain_note: the ruler or chief who leans on allies and forts

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no fortress for those who fear

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone whose own nerve fails, whatever backing he has

pazhamozhi.applied_to: allies and strength poured in from outside cannot save a man without courage of his own

286.reading: The verse says that an enemy who has risen against one, if rooted out swiftly while still young, does not grow mature, and that once all the friendships of those who had courted him are cut away he is left alone, for a lone tree never becomes a forest.
286.nuance: Two moves are joined: striking early (இளைதாய போழ்தே) and stripping the enemy of his allies (நண்பெல்லாந் தீர). The proverb proves the second: an enemy isolated cannot spread. The syntax of lines 2 and 3 is loose; தீர்த்து and தீர are read as the removal of the enemy and of his friends.
286.domain_note: the ruler facing a rising foe

pazhamozhi.literal: a single tree never becomes a forest

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to an enemy cut off from his allies

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an enemy isolated from his friends while still weak cannot grow into a threat

287.reading: The verse calls it folly to think of harming later those who have already harmed one greatly and risen in hostility, for, it tells a woman whose shoulders are like bamboo, no one ever takes the fangs of a snake that bites swiftly and runs.
287.nuance: The counsel is against putting off retaliation, not against retaliation: the snake that has bitten and fled cannot be caught afterwards, so the harm stands unanswered. The address to a woman (காம்பன்ன தோளி) frames a political counsel as talk to a beloved, as the hill and shore addresses do elsewhere.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one takes the tooth of a snake that has bitten and run

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to an enemy who strikes and withdraws

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who has been harmed must answer at once, since the chance passes with the attacker

288.reading: The verse appears to say that even the boundless great one entered hell after seeing it in full, that the pitiless do not relent, and closes with the proverb that when one comes to ruin the community, he is to be put away root and all.
288.nuance: The first two lines are hard to construe: who the வரம்பில் பெரியான் is and why he entered hell the verse does not say, and the link from that episode to the proverb is not plain. The proverb's own sense, that a destroyer of the kudi must be removed down to the foot, fits the heading on dealing with enemies; மன்றி may be a corruption.

pazhamozhi.literal: when one comes to ruin the people, cast him off till his foot is gone

story.act: a boundless great one entered hell after seeing it in full

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who would ruin the community is to be removed entirely, without pity

289.reading: The verse says that even when one shows favour to those who are not one's own, to men whose intent is not to be reconciled it plainly does not take, just as saline ground boils from within even when one mixes into it what makes good ground for a wall.
289.nuance: The fault is placed in the other's குறிப்பு, his settled intent, not in the favour shown: kindness cannot change a mind made up against one. The soil image makes the hostility a property of the ground itself, which treatment does not reach.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way saline ground boils within

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those whose intent is fixed against reconciliation

pazhamozhi.applied_to: favours to a settled enemy do not win him over

290.reading: The verse says that the wish of one who begs to be let into the house of those who cannot bear to see his face even outside is like a child crying to be carried on the hip by people who, on a great wilderness road, would not let him walk behind them on the proper path.
290.nuance: The proverb is a picture of misplaced asking: to want closeness (to be taken in, to be carried) from those who refuse even distance (to be seen, to be followed). The verse is about the asker's want of self-respect as much as the host's enmity; its link to the heading is through the hostile host.

pazhamozhi.literal: crying for the hip, as a child wails to be carried

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who seeks entry where he is hated

pazhamozhi.applied_to: seeking intimacy from those who cannot bear one's face is a child's futile wailing

291.reading: The verse says one should not seek enmity with the very great, for the demon who took it on without care was caught in battle, and even those who have the greatness of penance have never clapped Death on the back.
291.nuance: The example is a warning against one's own strength: the அரக்கன் is cast as a figure great in penance who still fell, so even power won by austerity does not make the great safe to offend. The proverb turns the point to death, which no penance mocks.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one ever clapped Death on the back

story.act: a demon who took on enmity with the great without heed was caught in war
story.tradition: identified by tradition as Ravana; the verse says only அரக்கன், fused with கொண்டு in கொண்டரக்கன்

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even those mighty by penance must not provoke the great, since none escapes the death that follows

292.reading: The verse says that the small, taking folly as their prop, behaving with hostility toward those who have attached themselves to the great, are, lord of the hill where the packs of wild dogs fear the noise, like the bear that by crying out rouses the fierce dog.
292.nuance: The target here is not the great but their dependents (பெரியாரைச் சார்ந்தார்), and the danger lies in waking the protector. எண்கு is the bear; புலம்புகின் is read as its crying out, though it may mean when it is alone.

pazhamozhi.literal: the bear rouses the fierce dog

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the small who provoke the dependents of the great

pazhamozhi.applied_to: attacking those under a great man's protection wakes the great man against oneself

293.reading: The verse says it is a danger for the weak to scorn those strong in strife and stand against them, and bids them go far off and survive by whatever means, for the man who does not die will yet touch the bangle on the forearm.
293.nuance: The counsel puts survival above standing: என்செய்தே யாயினும், by doing anything at all. The proverb's bangle is most plausibly the joys of later life (the embrace of a bangled arm), held out to the one who lives, so retreat is presented as a gain deferred, not a disgrace.

pazhamozhi.literal: the one who does not die will touch the bangle on the forearm

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the weak man who flees a stronger foe

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the weak should escape a strong enemy by any means, since the living may yet prosper

294.reading: The verse says that the small, standing with a single resource, doing many things to inflame those who stand victorious, is, lord of the hill where the bees war with the mountain, a thing that by no means comes out well.
294.nuance: The image is of the bees that sting the cliff on which they hang their hives: an attack that cannot hurt its target. ஒன்றொடு நின்று is read as the small man's single strength against the victor's many; line 1 is likely corrupt (நிற்பாறை for நிற்பாரை).

pazhamozhi.literal: it is not a thing that came with good

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the small who provoke the victorious

pazhamozhi.applied_to: provoking the proven strong ends in harm to the provoker

295.reading: The verse seems to say that those who rise roaring and swagger, asking whether a kite will not peck at the tongue of whoever spoke against them, if they fight and enrage men who do not swerve from what they have resolved, become the food of those who eat behind the offering.
295.nuance: Those who eat behind the bali offering are most plausibly the crows, so the swaggerers end as carrion. The quoted taunt in line 1 and the phrase இழைத்த திகவாதவர் (those who do not exceed what they set) are both hard; the reading follows the most likely sense.

pazhamozhi.literal: the food of those who eat outside the offering

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to boasters who provoke the steadfast

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those who swagger against firm men end up dead

296.reading: The verse says that as everything with a tuber sprouts in one way when it gets the cool rain of the thundering sky, one should not keep those one has come to favour coiled about one's roots, for old enmity never becomes friendship.
296.nuance: The tuber image explains why old enmity does not end: it lies dormant underground and sprouts as soon as its season comes. விழைந்தவரை is read as former enemies one has come to like; வேர்சுற்ற puts them at the root, the place where a sprouting tuber does most harm.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no old enmity that becomes friendship

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to reconciled enemies kept close

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a former enemy kept close will turn when his chance comes

297.reading: The verse asks what those who live elsewhere can do, even if a flood is the enemy, and says that a false, excessive friendship that has come close with deceit is like a debt eaten in one's own house.
297.nuance: The contrast is distance: an enemy as great as a flood harms those far off little, while the deceitful friend at hand consumes from within, as a debt run up in the house eats the household. அள்ளில்லம் is obscure; it is read as the near house, one's own.

pazhamozhi.literal: the debt eaten in the near house

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the deceitful friend at one's side

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a false friend close at hand is worse than a great enemy far off

links.note: Kural 750 says a fort with every excellence is nothing for those without excellence in action; Pazhamozhi 285 names the missing excellence as courage and adds allies to the fort as a support that fails without it.
links.teaches: Read together, the outer defences of a ruler, walls and allies alike, are shown to depend on one inner thing, and the Pazhamozhi names that thing as freedom from fear.
links.list_adds: it sets strong allies beside the fort as a second outer prop and lets the proverb make fear the single cause that empties both.

links.note: Kural 879 says to cut the thorn tree while young; Pazhamozhi 286 keeps the timing and adds a second step, stripping the young enemy of his friends.
links.teaches: The pair gives two parts of one tactic: the Kural's when (before the thorn hardens) and the Pazhamozhi's how (leave the tree alone so it cannot become a forest).
links.list_adds: it joins early action to isolation from allies, a pairing the couplet's single tree image does not make.

links.note: Kural 489 says to do the hard deed at the very moment the rare chance comes; Pazhamozhi 287 applies this to answering an enemy who has struck, and calls delay folly.
links.teaches: The Kural's general rule of the moment is given a hostile case, where the passing chance is the attacker himself, gone like a snake once it has bitten.
links.list_adds: it turns the couplet's abstract rare moment into a concrete one with a cost, the snake's fang that cannot be taken once it has fled.

links.note: Both verses urge acting at once against an enemy; 286 speaks of an enmity still young, 287 of one that has already struck.
links.teaches: Together they cover enmity before and after its first blow, and say that in neither case does waiting help, once because the enemy grows, once because he escapes.

links.note: Thirikadugam 24 makes the bowing of hardened enemies a mire; Pazhamozhi 289 says favours shown to enemies set against reconciliation do not take.
links.teaches: The two verses look at a false peace from both sides: the enemy's submission cannot be trusted, and one's own kindness cannot change him, so neither party's gesture ends a settled enmity.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 60 counts going before those who are not one's own as laughable; Pazhamozhi 290 says why, with the child crying to be carried by those who would not let it follow.
links.teaches: The counted line names the act as laughable; the proverb shows what makes it so, the asking for closeness from people who deny even distance.

links.note: Kural 269 says that even leaping past Death becomes possible for those who have gained the power of penance; Pazhamozhi 291 says that even those with the greatness of penance have never clapped Death on the back.
links.teaches: The two take opposite views of what penance can do against death: the Kural lets austerity overcome it, while the Pazhamozhi, using the demon great in penance who fell, denies that it protects the one who provokes the great.
links.list_adds: it sets the claim inside a story of a penitent who was destroyed in war, so the power of tapas is tested by a case rather than asserted.

links.note: Kural 892 says disregard of the great brings ills that do not leave; Pazhamozhi 291 gives an exemplary case, the demon who took enmity with the great without heed and was caught in battle.
links.teaches: The Kural's general warning gains a named example and a sharper premise, that the offender's own might, even might won by penance, does not change the outcome.
links.list_adds: it adds the exemplum and the point that the offender was himself great, which the couplet's plain contrast of the great and the heedless leaves out.

links.note: Naladiyar 178 says enemies' anger cannot reach the weak who have joined good protection, like grass by a stump the plough avoids; Pazhamozhi 292 says the small who attack such dependents only rouse the protector.
links.teaches: The same situation is seen from both sides: the quatrain promises the protected weak their safety, and the Pazhamozhi warns their attacker that striking them wakes the great one behind them.
links.list_adds: its bear and wild dog image shows the attacker's fate, which the quatrain's stump and plough, concerned only with the sheltered grass, does not.

links.note: 291 warns against enmity with the great themselves; 292 extends the warning to enmity with those who depend on the great.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the reach of a great man's protection is shown to cover his dependents, so the danger of provoking him begins one step before he is touched.

links.note: Kural 861 says to avoid opposing the strong; Pazhamozhi 293 says what the weak should do when the strong are already against them: flee far and live by any means.
links.teaches: The couplet only advises against the contest; the Pazhamozhi carries the advice into defeat and allows any means of escape, since survival keeps future good open.
links.list_adds: it adds the step of flight and the proverb's promise of later fortune, which the couplet's balanced rule for strong and weak lacks.

links.note: Kural 969 praises those who, like the yak, give up life when honour is at stake; Pazhamozhi 293 tells the weak to survive by doing anything at all.
links.teaches: The two give opposite answers on whether life may be bought with loss of standing: the Kural's man of honour dies rather than live shamed, while the Pazhamozhi counts staying alive as the greater good.
links.list_adds: its என்செய்தே யாயினும் and the promise of the bangle make survival a positive aim, where the couplet makes life itself forfeit to honour.

links.note: Kural 894 says that when the weak do harm to the strong it is like beckoning Death; Pazhamozhi 294 says the small inflaming the victorious ends in no good.
links.teaches: The Kural's image makes the attack fatal; the Pazhamozhi's bees warring with the mountain make it pointless as well, an assault that cannot even reach its target.
links.list_adds: it adds futility to danger: the bees' quarrel with the hill shows the attack does nothing to the strong, not only that it destroys the weak.

links.note: Thirikadugam 4 names living openly before enemies and taking by the hand one once enraged as the doings of a man about to die; Pazhamozhi 295 says those who swagger and enrage the steadfast become crows' food.
links.teaches: Both verses treat a way of behaving toward enemies as a sign of death already on its way, the counted work by naming it, the Pazhamozhi by showing the boaster's end as carrion.

links.note: Kural 874 says the world rests on the greatness of one who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship; Pazhamozhi 296 says old enmity never becomes friendship. On the reading that 874 means turning enemies into friends, the two conflict.
links.teaches: The two disagree over whether enmity can be converted: the Kural praises the man who makes a friend of a foe, while the Pazhamozhi holds that the old foe, like a tuber, only waits for rain.
links.list_adds: its tuber image gives a reason for the denial, that enmity lies dormant and revives with its season, which the couplet's praise does not face.

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu 17 names winning over those who are not one's allies as sweeter than doing good to the land; Pazhamozhi 296 says an old enemy never becomes a friend and should not be kept close.
links.teaches: Within the ethics group itself the two verses disagree on the reconciled enemy, one ranking his winning over among the sweetest things and the other counting him a sprout that will rise against one.

links.note: Kural 882 says not to fear sword-like enemies but the bond with kin-like ones; Pazhamozhi 297 gives the reason as distance, the flood afar against the debt in one's own house.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the ranking of the two dangers; the Pazhamozhi explains it, since the open enemy works from outside and far off while the false friend consumes the house from within.
links.list_adds: it sets a flood, a natural force, against a household debt, so the ranking turns on nearness rather than on the enemy's strength.

source_issues: 288 lines 1-2: the episode of the boundless great one entering hell is obscure, and மன்றி in the proverb may be corrupt.
289 line 4: the proverb has a closing quotation mark but no opening one.
294 line 1: நிற்பாறை is most likely a corruption of நிற்பாரை.
295 lines 1-3: the taunt and இழைத்த திகவாதவர் are of uncertain sense.
